opus-5.5.text:
Because the output is only the surface. Two networks can produce exactly the same image, pixel for pixel, and still be completely different underneath. And that difference is where everything interesting lives.

In our recent work, we took images from Picbreeder, where people evolved them through open-ended exploration, and compared those networks with ones trained by conventional SGD to produce the same image. When you look inside the Picbreeder networks, you see something remarkable. There's a beautiful, modular decomposition. One dimension of the network controls, say, the mouth of the skull opening and closing. Another handles symmetry. The pieces correspond to meaningful parts of the world. We call that a unified factored representation.

Then you look at the SGD network that produces the identical skull, and it's a mess. We call it fractured and entangled. Things that should be one concept are split into disconnected pieces, and things that should be separate are tangled together. If you perturb a weight, you don't get a meaningful variation of the skull. You just get garbage.

Why does that matter if the output is correct? Because what you ultimately care about isn't just reproducing what you've already seen. It's what happens next: generalization, creativity, continual learning, building on what you know. If your representation is fractured, then every step forward is harder, because the network doesn't really understand the structure of what it's doing. It's memorizing a facade. A well-factored representation is like having the right conceptual handles. It makes the adjacent possible accessible.

This is a warning about what you might call representational optimism, the assumption that if performance is good, the internals must be fine, and that scaling will clean things up. I think that's a dangerous assumption. Large models might be doing amazing things on benchmarks while carrying a lot of this fractured entanglement inside, and that could explain some of the strange failures we see. The way you get somewhere really does matter. And interestingly, in Picbreeder, the good representations emerged precisely because nobody was aiming for the final image. They were following interesting stepping stones, and that open-ended path seems to produce much deeper structure than direct optimization toward an objective.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, this is really the heart of what we found in the fractured entangled representation work. The thing is, if you only look at the output — the final image — you can be completely fooled. You've got two networks that both produce, say, the skull from Picbreeder, pixel for pixel essentially identical. From the outside, they look like they've learned the same thing. But they haven't. Not even close.

The Picbreeder network, the one that was discovered through this open-ended, serendipitous process of humans picking things that looked interesting, has this beautifully modular, decomposed internal representation. You can go in and sweep a single weight and the mouth opens and closes. Another weight and the eyes change. Everything is organized along the lines of the actual regularities in the thing it's representing. There's symmetry baked in, there's a sense of what the parts are.

Now take the network trained with SGD to reproduce that exact same image. It gets there. The loss goes to zero. But when you look inside, it's a mess. The representation is what we call fractured and entangled — the concepts are smeared across weights, the symmetry isn't actually represented as symmetry, it's just two halves that happen to coincide. Sweep a weight and you get this chaotic, nonsensical distortion, because nothing in there corresponds to anything meaningful about skulls.

And the reason this matters is that the representation is what determines everything downstream. It determines whether you can generalize, whether you can learn the next thing efficiently, whether you can be creative. If you want to make a new skull with a different expression, the Picbreeder network can do it trivially — the knob is right there. The SGD network can't, because it never built the abstraction. It just memorized a path to the answer.

So I think the deeper point is that we've been grading these systems almost entirely on the destination, and the destination can hide a profound difference in understanding. Two systems can have the same performance and radically different capacities for what comes after. And I'd argue that's a warning for the field more broadly — hitting the benchmark is not the same as having a good representation, and the way you got there, the process, leaves a fingerprint on what's inside.

astra-6.text:
Because reproducing the image doesn’t necessarily mean reproducing the discovery. You can take the final image as a target and train a network to match it, and that network might do a very good job. But that tells you something different from how the image arose in Picbreeder, where people were choosing things they found interesting without knowing what the eventual result would be.

The path matters because it shapes the representation inside the network. Two networks can produce nearly identical images, yet behave very differently when you mutate them. In one, a small change might alter a coherent feature while preserving the rest of the image. In the other, changes might be much less coherent. So matching the pixels doesn’t tell you whether you’ve captured the same potential for further evolution.

That’s the deeper issue: an outcome is also a stepping stone. If we judge only how closely a network matches a particular image, we can miss what makes it a productive starting point for discovering something else.

sol-6.1.text:
Because reproducing the image doesn’t necessarily reproduce the process that made it discoverable. You can give a neural network the final image as a target and optimize until it looks right, but that doesn’t tell you whether it passed through useful stepping stones along the way.

In Picbreeder, people aren’t usually trying to reach a particular final image. They see something interesting, select it, and then discover something else they couldn’t have anticipated. An image that eventually becomes a butterfly might have been selected earlier for a feature that had nothing to do with butterflies.

So the path matters because it reveals how new possibilities arise. If we only ask whether an algorithm can reproduce the endpoint, we can miss the very thing we’re trying to understand: how you discover something when you don’t yet know what you’re looking for.
